analysis.one_liner: Restores the DEA's power to quickly shut down drug companies suspected of fueling the opioid epidemic.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in October 2017 and died there without ever receiving a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended, despite bipartisan sponsorship from 1 Republican and 7 Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2016, Congress changed the drug-control law so the DEA could no longer move immediately against a drug company whose shipments posed an "imminent danger" to public health; instead, companies got notice and time to submit a corrective plan before their license to handle controlled substances could be suspended or revoked. This bill repeals those changes, giving the DEA back its faster enforcement tools against manufacturers, wholesale distributors, and pharmacies suspected of over-shipping opioid painkillers. It never received a vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit hard by opioid overdoses, where pill mills and suspiciously large orders of prescription painkillers fueled addiction; DEA and local enforcement get back the ability to freeze a company's registration quickly, before shipments accumulate.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2016 amendments that required the government to give a registrant notice and an opportunity to file a corrective action plan before a registration could be revoked or suspended, restoring the DEA's faster process.
Restores the DEA's authority to act when there is an "imminent danger to the public health or safety," striking the 2016 language that limited when immediate suspension orders could issue.

Strikes the new registration factors added by the 2016 Act, restoring the pre-2016 standards the DEA used to decide whether manufacturers, distributors, and dispensers may handle controlled substances.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers, wholesale distributors, and pharmacies would face easier and faster DEA enforcement, including immediate suspension of the registrations they need to ship or dispense controlled substances; some legitimate pharmacies could lose access to medications temporarily while disputing an order.

drawbacks.text: The 2016 changes were promoted as protecting patient access: the pre-revocation notice and corrective-action-plan window was meant to prevent the DEA from cutting off legitimate pharmacies and distributors on thin evidence, which would interrupt supply of lawful pain and other controlled medications to patients.

A blanket repeal of the 2016 sections, rather than a targeted fix, removes all of the procedural protections the 2016 Act created for registrants, raising the risk that pharmacies and manufacturers acting in good faith face suspension orders before they can respond.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health stakes are large: faster DEA action against suspicious opioid shipments addresses the supply side of an epidemic that was devastating communities. The costs are real but narrower: legitimate pharmacies and distributors could be suspended before getting a chance to correct problems, temporarily interrupting patient access to controlled medications. On balance, the public benefits of restoring immediate-suspension authority outweigh the access risks, which could have been addressed in a more tailored bill — one that never got written or voted on here.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees in October 2017, sent to two subcommittees, and no markup or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ann Kuster of New Hampshire introduced the bill on October 19, 2017, joined as original cosponsors by Rep. Evan Jenkins of West Virginia, Rep. Tim Ryan of Ohio, and Rep. Jim Cooper of Tennessee.

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee, then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; the action record shows no further action.

The bill would repeal Sections 1 and 2 of the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2016 and the amendments they made to the Controlled Substances Act, which had modified the DEA's registration and enforcement authorities over manufacturers, distributors, and dispensers of controlled substances.
The 8 cosponsors included 7 Democrats and 1 Republican; no vote was ever recorded in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The drug distribution and manufacturing industry kept the slower, notice-and-corrective-plan enforcement regime created by the 2016 law, because the repeal never advanced.

against.what_they_did: Favored keeping the 2016 enforcement changes that this bill would repeal, which a major 2017 news investigation reported they had lobbied for; the industry did not need to act on this bill because it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew cosponsors from both parties — 7 Democrats and 1 Republican among the 8 — but the only decisive action was inaction in committee, where no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The 2016 law gave distributors notice and a corrective-plan window before the DEA could suspend or revoke their registration, slowing action on suspicious opioid shipments; repeal would have restored the immediate-suspension tool. Keeping that protection was worth billions in opioid shipping revenue that faster enforcement would have put at risk.

Repeal would have made it easier for the DEA to deny, suspend, or revoke a manufacturer's registration under the restored standards. Most manufacturers ship legitimate products, so the risk to them is indirect — mainly faster enforcement against bad actors in the supply chain.

Pharmacies also lost the corrective-action-plan protection the 2016 Act created, since it applied to dispensers as well as manufacturers and distributors. Some legitimate pharmacies could face suspension before getting a chance to respond, temporarily cutting patient access.
